'''Heather D. Willauer''' (born 1974) is an American [[Analytical chemistry|analytical chemist]] and [[inventor]] working in [[Washington, D.C.]], at the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]] (NRL). Leading a research team, Willauer has patented a method for removing dissolved [[carbon dioxide]] (CO<sub>2</sub>) from [[seawater]], in parallel with [[hydrogen]] (H<sub>2</sub>) recovered by conventional [[Electrolysis of water|water electrolysis]]. Willauer is also searching to improve the [[catalyst]]s required to enable a continuous [[Fischer–Tropsch process]] to recombine [[carbon monoxide]] (CO) and [[hydrogen]] gases into complex [[hydrocarbon]] liquids to [[Synthetic fuel|synthesize jet fuel]] for Navy aircraft.

Especially significant for the Navy is the possibility of maintaining [[Naval aviation|naval air operations]] in remote areas without depending too much on long-distance transport of jet fuel across oceans. The Navy is also studying the feasibility of constructing on-shore facilities capable of synthesizing [[kerosene]] from [[hydrogen]] and [[Carbon dioxide|CO<sub>2</sub>]], both extracted from [[seawater]] constituents. Because of the very high electrical power required by [[Electrolysis of water|water electrolysis]] to produce considerable amounts of hydrogen, nuclear power plants or [[ocean thermal energy conversion]] (OTEC) are necessary to fuel the industrial installations built on-shore on remote islands close to the sea in strategic locations.

==Education==
Willauer attended [[Berry College]] in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], graduating with a bachelor's degree in chemistry in 1996.<ref name=Larson2013>{{cite web |url=http://energyfromthorium.com/2013/06/16/opportunities-in-nuclear/ |title=Opportunities in Nuclear – Second Annual Ohio State University Nuclear Power Forum, September 19, 2013 |date=June 16, 2013 |last=Larson |first=Don |publisher=Energy from Thorium Foundation |access-date=June 18, 2014 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> In mid-1999 she participated in the 11th International Conference on Partitioning in Aqueous Two-Phase Systems, held in [[Gulf Shores, Alabama]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://bama.ua.edu/~rdrogers/aq2phase/Participants11.pdf |title=List of Participants |publisher=11th International Conference on Partitioning in Aqueous Two-Phase Systems |date=June 27 – July 2, 1999 |location=Gulf Shores, Alabama |access-date=June 17, 2014 |archive-date=May 18, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080518074411/http://bama.ua.edu/~rdrogers/aq2phase/Participants11.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2002, she earned a doctorate in [[analytical chemistry]] from the [[University of Alabama]], writing her thesis on "Fundamentals of phase behavior and solute partitioning in ABS and applications to the paper industry," the "ABS" an abbreviation for "[[Aqueous two-phase system|aqueous biphasic systems]]".<ref>{{cite thesis |url=http://library.ua.edu/vwebv/holdingsInfo?bibId=1556675 |title=Fundamentals of phase behavior and solute partitioning in ABS and applications to the paper industry |last=Willauer |first=Heather D. |publisher=University of Alabama, Department of Chemistry |location=Tuscaloosa, Alabama |date=2002}}</ref> She began working with the NRL as an associate, then in 2004 she advanced to the position of research chemist.<ref name=Larson2013/>

==Career==
Willauer started researching [[Phase (matter)|biphasic systems]] and [[phase transition]]s after graduating from Berry College. In 1998 she studied aqueous biphasic systems (ABS) for the potential of recapturing valuable dyes from textile manufacturing effluent. She investigated [[ion]]s and [[catalyst]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Separation and recovery of food coloring dyes using aqueous biphasic extraction chromatographic resins |author=Jonathan G. Huddleston |author2=Heather D. Willauer |author3=Kathy R. Boaz |author4=Robin D. Rogers |journal=[[Journal of Chromatography B]] |volume=711 |number=1–2 |date=26 June 1998 |pages=237–244 |doi=10.1016/S0378-4347(97)00662-2|pmid=9699992 }}</ref>

[[File:Heather Willauer at NRL.jpg|thumb|Willauer at the NRL]]
In the 2000s, Willauer began studying methods for extracting CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> from seawater, for the purpose of reacting these molecules into hydrocarbons by using the [[Fischer–Tropsch process]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.nrl.navy.mil/media/news-releases/2012/fueling-the-fleet-navy-looks-to-the-seas |title=Fueling the Fleet, Navy Looks to the Seas |last=Parry |first=Daniel |date=September 24, 2012 |work=Naval Research Laboratory News |access-date=June 18, 2014 |archive-date=February 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180203162405/https://www.nrl.navy.mil/media/news-releases/2012/fueling-the-fleet-navy-looks-to-the-seas |url-status=dead }}</ref> She also investigated modified [[iron]] (Fe) [[Catalysis|catalyst]]s and studied [[zeolite]] (nanoporous [[aluminosilicate]]) catalyst supports for recombining these molecules into jet fuel.

Previous studies had concluded that CO<sub>2</sub>, under the form of the bicarbonate anion (HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>) dominant (96% [[mole fraction]]) in the seawater inorganic carbon species could not be economically removed from seawater.<ref name="Willauer_2010">{{cite journal |title=Synfuel from Seawater |author=H.D. Willauer |author2=D.R. Hardy |author3=F. DiMascio |author4=R.W. Dorner |author5=F.W. Williams |date=2010 |journal=NRL Review |publisher=United States Naval Research Laboratory |pages=153–154 |url=http://www.nrl.navy.mil/content_images/2010_NRL_Review.revised.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130306055242/http://www.nrl.navy.mil/content_images/2010_NRL_Review.revised.pdf |archive-date=March 6, 2013 |access-date=July 15, 2021}} </ref> However, by acidifying seawater by means of an adapted electrolysis cell with cation permeable membranes (dubbed a three-chambered electrochemical acidification cell),<ref name="Szondy_2012" /> it is possible to economically convert HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> into CO<sub>2</sub> at a pH lower than 6 and to increase the extraction yield. In January 2011, the NRL installed a prototype of seawater electrolysis cell at [[Naval Air Station Key West]] in Florida.<ref name="Parry2014">{{cite news |url=http://www.nrl.navy.mil/media/news-releases/2014/scale-model-wwii-craft-takes-flight-with-fuel-from-the-sea-concept |title=Scale Model WWII Craft Takes Flight With Fuel From the Sea Concept |last=Parry |first=Daniel |date=April 7, 2014 |work=Naval Research Laboratory News  |access-date=June 18, 2014 |archive-date=August 22, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170822074801/https://www.nrl.navy.mil/media/news-releases/2014/scale-model-wwii-craft-takes-flight-with-fuel-from-the-sea-concept }}</ref>

In 2017, Willauer ''et al.'' were granted a patent for a {{CO2}} extraction device from seawater, in the form of an electrolytic-[[Ion|cation]] exchange module (E-CEM). The E-CEM is seen as a "key step" in the production of synthetic fuel from seawater. Other researchers named in the patent are Felice DiMascio, Dennis R. Hardy, Jeffrey Baldwin, Matthew Bradley, James Morris, Ramagopal Ananth and Frederick W. Williams.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nrl.navy.mil/Media/News/releases/nrl-receives-us-patent-carbon-capture-device-key-step-synthetic-fuel-production-seawater/ |last=Parry |first=Daniel |date=October 3, 2017 |title=NRL Receives US Patent for Carbon Capture Device: A Key Step in Synthetic Fuel Production from Seawater |website=Naval Research Laboratory |access-date=July 22, 2020}}</ref>

==Feasibility of jet fuel synthesis==
Willauer ''et al.'' (2012) estimated that jet fuel could be synthesized from seawater in quantities up to {{convert|100000|gal|L|abbr=on}} per day, at a cost of three to six U.S. dollars per gallon.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Willauer |first1=Heather |last2=Morse |first2=James |last3=Baldwin |first3=Jeffrey |title=6.1 New Start: Conversion of CO2 Waste Into Energetic Molecules (FY15-FY19) |url=https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/AD1120876.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211006135913/https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/AD1120876.pdf |url-status=live |archive-date=October 6, 2021 |website=NRL |publisher=Naval Research Laboratory |access-date=25 January 2022}}</ref><ref name="Feasibility_2012">{{cite journal |title=The feasibility and current estimated capital costs of producing jet fuel at sea using carbon dioxide and hydrogen |author1=Heather D. Willauer |author2=Dennis R. Hardy |author3=Kenneth R. Schultz |author4=Frederick W. Williams |journal= Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy|volume=4 |page= 033111 |number=33111 |date=2012 |doi=10.1063/1.4719723|s2cid= 109523882 }}</ref><ref name="Szondy_2012">{{cite journal |url=http://www.gizmag.com/jet-fuel-seawater/24287/ |title=U.S. Navy looking at obtaining fuel from seawater |last=Szondy |first=David |date=September 26, 2012 |journal=GizMag}}</ref> Willauer ''et al.'' (2014) showed that the Fischer-Tropsch catalyst could be modified to synthesize various fuels such as [[methanol]] and [[natural gas]], as well as the [[olefins]] that can be used as the building blocks for jet fuel.

Willauer ''et al.'' calculated that about {{convert|23000|gal|L|abbr=on}} of seawater must be driven through the process to obtain the quantities of hydrogen and CO<sub>2</sub> necessary to synthesize one gallon of jet fuel.

Seawater was chosen because it contains 140 times more CO<sub>2</sub> by volume than the atmosphere, and conventional water electrolysis also yields H<sub>2</sub>. The equipment for processing seawater is much smaller than that for processing air. Willauer considered that seawater was the "best option" for a source of synthetic jet fuel.<ref name="Tozer2014">{{cite web |first=Jessica L. |last=Tozer |title=Energy Independence: Creating Fuel from Seawater |date=April 11, 2014 |work=Armed with Science |publisher=U.S. Department of Defense |url=http://science.dodlive.mil/2014/04/11/energy-independence-creating-fuel-from-sea-water/  |access-date=July 10, 2021 |archive-date=April 12, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140412160125/http://science.dodlive.mil/2014/04/11/energy-independence-creating-fuel-from-sea-water/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.nationaljournal.com/innovation-works/guess-what-could-fuel-the-battleships-of-the-future-20131213 |title=Guess What Could Fuel the Battleships of the Future? |last=Koren |first=Marina |date=December 13, 2013 |journal=National Journal}}{{Closed access}}{{Password-protected}}</ref> By April 2014, the Willauer's team had not yet made fuel to the quality standard required for military jets,<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.defenseone.com/technology/2014/04/navy-just-turned-seawater-jet-fuel/82300/ |title=The Navy Just Turned Seawater Into Jet Fuel |date=April 10, 2014 |last=Tucker |first=Patrick |journal=Defense One}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2014/apr/10/game-changer-us-navy-can-now-turn-seawater-jet-fue/ |title=U.S. Navy to turn seawater into jet fuel |date=April 10, 2014 |last=Ernst |first=Douglas |newspaper=The Washington Times}}</ref> but they were able in September 2013 to use the fuel to fly a radio-controlled model airplane powered by a common two-stroke [[internal combustion engine]].<ref name="Parry2014" />

Because the process requires a considerable input of electrical energy<ref name="Feasibility_2012" /> (~ 250 MW electricity mainly for the H<sub>2</sub> production by water electrolysis and also to a lesser extent for the CO<sub>2</sub> recovery from seawater),<ref name="Feasibility_2012" /> it cannot be performed on a large ship, even on a nuclear aircraft-carrier. The installations processing seawater to obtain H<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> (in fact CO),  the two essential ingredients necessary for the [[Fischer–Tropsch process]], must be constructed on-shore, close to the sea, on islands in strategic remote locations (''e.g.'', [[Hawaii|Hawai]], [[Guam]], [[Diego Garcia|Diego-Garcia]]) and powered by a nuclear reactor, or by [[ocean thermal energy conversion]] (OTEC).
